\chapter{One and the Other}
\label{ch:hi-one-and-the-other}
\hlchaptermodality{84}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say one thing and the other with ek and dusra, and tell that apart from naming a thing's place in a line.}

The ordinals and ek ... dusra worked on the same set, so the difference between naming a place and sorting two things is done rather than stated.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ek … dūsrā]{\hi{एक} … \hi{दूसरा} (ek … dūsrā) — one and the other}

\label{lesson:HI-C77-one-other}



\begin{quote}
Recalls open the chapter's last stretch, at the four measured distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dasvā̃} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{chaṭhā} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{jab … tab …} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{-kar} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kuttā} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{when to say śubh sandhyā} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one, and the other}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{एक} … \hi{दूसरा}} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one … the other}\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{किताब} \hi{नई} \hi{है}, \hi{दूसरी} \hi{पुरानी।}} — One book is new, the other old. \textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{आदमी} \hi{यहाँ} \hi{है}, \hi{दूसरा} \hi{वहाँ।}} — One man is here, the other there.
\end{quote}

The second ordinal lesson said to hold both senses of \textbf{\hi{दूसरा}} together, and this is why. Hindi needs no third word to say \textquotedblleft{}one … the other\textquotedblright{}: it puts \textbf{\hi{एक}} in the first half and \textbf{\hi{दूसरा}} in the second, and the second sense of \emph{dūsrā} does the rest.

Both halves agree with what they name, so a feminine noun gives \textbf{\hi{एक} … \hi{दूसरी}}.

That is a thing worth having. Sorting two of anything — two books, two men, two roads — needs this and nothing else.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ek … dūsrā}
  \item \emph{ek kitāb merī hai, dūsrī uskī} — one book is mine, the other is his
  \item \emph{ek ādmī andar thā, dūsrā bāhar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Hindi say \textquotedblleft{}one … the other\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\hi{एक} … \hi{दूसरा}} — no third word.) Which sense of \emph{dūsrā} is doing the work? (\textbf{Other}, not \emph{second}.) And what changes for a feminine noun? (\textbf{\hi{दूसरी}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pahlā, dūsrā, tīsrā …]{Putting things in order — the ordinals and \hi{एक} … \hi{दूसरा} together}

\label{lesson:HI-C77-practice}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, and then the work of the last three chapters: everything in one place.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ek … dūsrā} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sātvā̃} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{saknā} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kyā …?} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{billī} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{śubh dopahar} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: two ways of ordering}
You have ten ordinals, an ending that makes the rest, and \textbf{\hi{एक} … \hi{दूसरा}}. They do two different jobs, and the difference is easiest to feel on one small set.

Three books on a shelf:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{पहली} \hi{किताब}}, \textbf{\hi{दूसरी} \hi{किताब}}, \textbf{\hi{तीसरी} \hi{किताब}} — the first, second and third. Each one is named by \textbf{where it sits}, and the naming works however many there are.
  \item \textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{किताब} \hi{नई} \hi{है}, \hi{दूसरी} \hi{पुरानी।}} — One is new, the other old. Nothing is numbered; two things are \textbf{sorted against each other}, and this only works when there are two.
\end{itemize}

So: \textbf{\hi{पहले}} the first, and after it the second. Say the three books in order, then say the two-book version, and you have used both systems on the same shelf.

\textbf{\hi{पहला} \hi{दिन}}, \textbf{\hi{दूसरा} \hi{दिन}}, \textbf{\hi{तीसरा} \hi{दिन}} — and if you can say those, you can say the fortieth, because the ending does not stop.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three books — \emph{pahlī, dūsrī, tīsrī kitāb}
  \item the two books — \emph{ek kitāb merī hai, dūsrī uskī}
  \item \emph{pahlā din, dūsrā din, tīsrā din}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does an ordinal name? (\textbf{Where a thing sits in a line}.) What does \emph{ek … dūsrā} do instead? (\textbf{Sorts two things against each other}.) And how many things does that second one work for? (\textbf{Two}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
